name: Traceability Matrix - DRP
headers: Original Suggested ICT DR Policy Section
rows: Governance, risk appetite, ownership and oversight
PGPA Act s15 - duty to govern the Commonwealth entity
Requires accountable authorities to govern the entity in a way that promotes proper use and management of public resources, achievement of purposes and financial sustainability.
ICT DR is a core control supporting proper management of public resources and continuity of statutory services during disruptive events.
Directly applicable to NDIA governance and Board/accountable authority oversight.

- The ICT DR Policy must be approved, owned and reviewed under NDIA governance arrangements.
- ICT DR capability must be treated as a core enabler of NDIA's statutory service delivery and proper use of public resources.
Department of Finance / Federal Register of Legislation
Governance, risk appetite, ownership and oversight
PGPA Act s16 - duty to establish and maintain systems relating to risk and control
Requires appropriate systems of risk oversight, risk management and internal control.
DR relies on risk-based controls: BIA, criticality, RTO/RPO, backup, restoration, failover, incident recovery and supplier assurance.
Directly applicable to NDIA enterprise and ICT risk management.

- ICT DR risks must be identified, assessed, treated, monitored and reported through NDIA risk management processes.
- Critical systems must have documented and tested recovery controls proportionate to business impact and information sensitivity.
Department of Finance / Federal Register of Legislation
Records continuity, audit evidence, metadata, FOI and performance reporting
PGPA Act ss35, 37 and 39 - performance information, records and performance statements
Requires performance planning, records and reporting arrangements that can be evidenced.
DR policy must preserve availability and integrity of records used to evidence delivery, outage impacts and recovery performance.
Directly applicable to systems supporting NDIS performance, claims, participant planning and reporting.

- ICT DR events, tests and recoveries must generate auditable records sufficient to support performance and accountability reporting.
- Recovery reporting must capture service impact, outage duration, decisions, exceptions and lessons learned.
Department of Finance / Federal Register of Legislation
Backups, restoration, immutable recovery and transaction integrity
PGPA Act s41 - accounts and records
Requires proper accounts and records to be kept, including records explaining transactions and financial position.
Financial and payment systems must be recoverable with transaction integrity, reconciliation and auditability.
Directly applicable to NDIA payment, claims, provider and finance systems.
Data integrity and financial transaction recovery

- DR plans for financial and payment systems must include reconciliation, transaction integrity checks and approval controls before service restoration.
- Backup and recovery arrangements must protect records required to explain NDIA transactions.
Department of Finance / Federal Register of Legislation
DR testing, audit, accessibility validation and remediation tracking
PGPA Act s45 and PGPA Rule audit committee requirements
Supports independent assurance over risk, performance and accountability systems.
DR capability should be testable and reportable to management and audit committees as part of internal control assurance.
Directly applicable to NDIA audit and risk governance.

- ICT DR maturity, test results, exceptions and material risks must be reported to relevant NDIA governance and assurance forums.
- Internal audit and assurance activities may review compliance with this policy and the effectiveness of DR controls.
Department of Finance / Federal Register of Legislation
Governance, risk appetite, ownership and oversight
CRMP - accountable authority responsibility for risk management
Requires entities to embed risk management into governance, planning, decision-making and performance.
DR policy decisions need explicit risk appetite, risk ownership and escalation paths for residual outage and data-loss risks.
Applies as best practice for NDIA; PGPA s16 makes risk oversight and control directly relevant.

- NDIA must define risk appetite and tolerances for ICT service unavailability, data loss and recovery workarounds.
- Residual DR risks outside tolerance must be escalated and accepted only by authorised NDIA officers.
Governance, risk appetite, ownership and oversight
CRMP - risk management capability and culture
Requires fit-for-purpose risk capability and clear responsibilities.
A DR policy is ineffective unless business, ICT, cyber, privacy, records and supplier roles are assigned and exercised.
Applicable across NDIA business areas, ICT operations, cyber security, privacy, records and third-party management.

- Each critical business service must have an accountable business owner and ICT recovery owner.
- Personnel with DR responsibilities must be trained and participate in scheduled exercises.
Governance, risk appetite, ownership and oversight
Requires risk information to support monitoring, escalation and improvement.
DR metrics such as RTO/RPO compliance, backup success, test outcomes and unresolved risks must be reported.
Applicable to NDIA executive reporting and operational dashboards.

- ICT DR performance must be measured using agreed indicators including backup success, restore success, RTO/RPO achievement and exercise remediation closure.
- Material DR weaknesses must be recorded in risk registers with accountable owners and target remediation dates.
Critical services, BIA, RTO/RPO and service continuity scope
NDIS Act - establishment, functions and service delivery responsibilities
Establishes the National Disability Insurance Agency and the legislative framework for administering the NDIS.
DR policy must protect continuity of core NDIS functions, including participant access, planning, payments and provider interactions.
Directly applicable to all ICT systems supporting NDIS administration.

- ICT DR scope must prioritise systems and data supporting participant access, reasonable and necessary supports, plan administration, claims and provider payments.
- Business impact assessments must consider impact on people with disability, nominees, providers and staff.
Department of Social Services / Federal Register of Legislation
Personal information, NDIS protected information, data sharing and classification controls
NDIS Act - use and disclosure of protected information
Contains confidentiality and information-handling obligations for information collected in NDIS administration.
DR activities must not weaken confidentiality while restoring availability; emergency access, backups and test data must remain controlled.
Directly applicable to production, backup, replicated, archived and test environments containing participant information.
Protected information and privacy during recovery

- Recovery activities must preserve confidentiality of NDIS protected information in all copies, backups, replicas and DR environments.
- Emergency access used during recovery must be approved, logged, reviewed and revoked when no longer required.
Department of Social Services / Federal Register of Legislation
Accessible, inclusive and properly marked DR communications and workarounds
The scheme depends on reliable information and service channels for participants, nominees, providers and staff.
DR policy must prioritise continuity and accessible alternatives for vulnerable users during ICT disruption.
Applicable to my NDIS, participant portals, provider portals, contact centres and internal case systems.

- DR planning must include accessible communications and alternative service channels for participants and providers during ICT outages.
- Recovery priorities must account for critical participant needs and potential harm from service interruption.
Department of Social Services / Federal Register of Legislation
Personal information, NDIS protected information, data sharing and classification controls
NDIS Information Rules - protection and disclosure of information
Sets rules about how protected NDIS information may be handled and disclosed.
DR creates additional copies, access pathways and supplier touchpoints; policy must constrain these to authorised purposes.
Directly applicable to backup repositories, replication targets, DR runbooks, support access and recovery communications.

- NDIS protected information must only be accessed or disclosed during DR activities where authorised and necessary for recovery.
- DR runbooks must define who may access protected information and what approvals, logging and post-event reviews are required.
NDIS (Protection and Disclosure of Information) Rules 2013
Department of Social Services / Federal Register of Legislation
Third-party DR assurance, contracts and supplier conduct
NDIS Information Rules - secure handling by delegates, staff and service providers
Requires controls around access, disclosure and information sharing arrangements.
Suppliers that host, back up or restore NDIA systems may handle protected information and must be contractually controlled.
Applicable to managed service providers, cloud providers, recovery vendors and support teams.

- Contracts and operational procedures for DR suppliers must preserve NDIS protected-information obligations.
- Supplier personnel access to DR systems must be least privilege, time-bound, logged and reviewable.
NDIS (Protection and Disclosure of Information) Rules 2013
Department of Social Services / Federal Register of Legislation
DR activation, cyber recovery, ransomware response and breach notification
Procedures are developed, implemented and maintained to ensure security incidents are responded to and managed.
Direct DR dependency: recovery from cyber, physical or personnel-security events requires documented incident procedures so recovery is controlled, authorised and auditable.
Applicable. NDIA ICT services support participant, provider, payment and corporate functions; the DR policy must align recovery activation with security incident management and escalation.
Incident management interface and DR activation

NDIA must maintain and test procedures that define how ICT security incidents are triaged, escalated, contained, recovered and closed, including roles for ICT, Cyber Security, business service owners, suppliers and communications.
DR activation, cyber recovery, ransomware response and breach notification
Security incident management and response plans are incorporated into the entity's business continuity arrangements.
Security incident response must be embedded in business continuity so DR actions are aligned to business priorities, crisis communications and participant-facing service continuity.
Applicable. NDIA ICT DR planning must integrate with NDIA business continuity and crisis management arrangements for critical NDIS services.
Integration with business continuity and crisis management

The ICT DR Plan and security incident response plans must be integrated with NDIA business continuity arrangements, including common activation criteria, impact assessment, recovery priorities, escalation paths and post-incident review.
DR activation, cyber recovery, ransomware response and breach notification
Significant or externally reportable security incidents and referral obligations are reported to the relevant authority (or authorities) within the applicable timeframe.

DR incidents may trigger reporting to relevant cyber, privacy, protective security, law-enforcement, ministerial or other authorities; timeframes and accountabilities need to be embedded in the policy.
Applicable. NDIA handles sensitive participant and scheme information; the DR policy must ensure externally reportable cyber/security incidents are identified and notified within required timeframes.

NDIA must maintain a notification matrix for significant or externally reportable ICT/security incidents, specifying authorities, internal owners, evidence requirements, approval points and reporting timeframes.
Governance, risk appetite, ownership and oversight
The Accountable Authority determines their entity's tolerance for security risks and documents in the security plan.
Recovery objectives and residual-risk decisions must be set against documented security risk tolerance; without tolerance settings, RTO/RPO and exception decisions are ungoverned.
Applicable. NDIA's Accountable Authority risk tolerance should govern DR scope, recovery tiers, exceptions and acceptance of residual unavailability or data-loss risk.
Governance, risk tolerance and recovery objectives

NDIA's Accountable Authority must determine and approve the security and operational risk tolerance that underpins ICT DR planning, including maximum tolerable outage, recovery time objectives, recovery point objectives and risk acceptance thresholds.
Governance, risk appetite, ownership and oversight
A risk steward (or manager) is identified for each security risk or category of security risk, including shared risks.
Every DR risk needs an accountable owner; shared, platform and supplier risks need clear stewardship across business, ICT, security and providers.
Applicable. NDIA DR risks span internal ICT teams, Cyber Security, business owners and outsourced providers; stewardship must be explicit.

Each material ICT DR risk, shared risk and supplier dependency must have an identified risk steward or owner responsible for treatment plans, residual-risk acceptance, monitoring, testing evidence and reporting.
Governance, risk appetite, ownership and oversight
The Accountable Authority considers the impact that their security risk management decisions could potentially have on other entities, and shares information on risks where appropriate.
DR choices can affect other entities, partners, providers and participants; dependencies with shared services and whole-of-government platforms require risk sharing.
Applicable. NDIA relies on and exchanges data with government, partners, providers and service channels; DR decisions should consider downstream and upstream impacts.

NDIA must assess whether ICT DR decisions, outages, degraded operation or alternate processing arrangements create security or service-continuity risks for other entities and share relevant risk information through approved channels.
Third-party DR assurance, contracts and supplier conduct

The entity is accountable for the management of security risks arising from procuring goods and services and ensures procurement and contract decisions do not expose the entity or the Australian Government to an unacceptable level of risk.
Critical DR capabilities are often delivered through managed services, cloud, data centres and software; procurement decisions must not create unacceptable recovery or security risk.
Applicable. NDIA must manage ICT vendor and cloud-provider risks that affect resilience of NDIS systems, data, backups and recovery facilities.

Procurement and contract decisions for ICT services supporting DR must include security, resilience, data-protection, recovery and exit risks, and must not expose NDIA or the Australian Government to unacceptable risk.
Third-party DR assurance, contracts and supplier conduct

Procurement, contracts and third-party outsourced arrangements contain proportionate security terms and conditions to ensure service providers, contractors and subcontractors comply with relevant PSPF Requirements.
Contracts must contain enforceable DR and security terms so providers and subcontractors implement required recovery, testing, reporting and security controls.
Applicable. NDIA outsourced ICT, cloud, hosting and support arrangements must include DR obligations matched to business impact and data sensitivity.
Supplier contractual DR and security requirements

ICT contracts and outsourced arrangements must include proportionate security and DR terms covering availability, recovery objectives, backup retention, restoration testing, incident reporting, subcontractor controls, audit rights and compliance with relevant PSPF-aligned requirements.
Third-party DR assurance, contracts and supplier conduct
Entity ensures service providers, contractors and subcontractors comply with relevant PSPF Requirements as detailed by the entity.
Policy must ensure supplier compliance is actively managed, not assumed, because recovery capability depends on external controls operating as designed.
Applicable. NDIA must assure that suppliers supporting critical ICT services can meet DR and security obligations.

NDIA must require service providers, contractors and subcontractors supporting ICT DR to comply with NDIA-specified PSPF, ISM, Essential Eight, IRAP, hosting and contract-security obligations applicable to their services.
Third-party DR assurance, contracts and supplier conduct

Contractual security terms and conditions require service providers to report any actual or suspected security incidents to the entity, and follow reasonable direction from the entity arising from incident investigations.
Supplier incident reporting is essential for timely DR activation, containment, evidence preservation and coordinated investigation.
Applicable. Many NDIA ICT incidents may be first detected by cloud, managed-service, application or data-centre providers.

Contracts for ICT and DR-related services must require suppliers to promptly report actual or suspected security incidents, preserve evidence, support NDIA investigations and follow reasonable NDIA directions during containment, recovery and review.
Third-party DR assurance, contracts and supplier conduct
Government entities providing outsourced services provide IRAP assessment reports to the government entities consuming, or looking to consume, their services.
IRAP reports for government-provided outsourced services provide assurance that consumed platforms can securely recover and operate.
Conditional. Applies where NDIA consumes or provides outsourced/shared government ICT services; DR policy should require IRAP evidence before relying on those services for recovery.

Where NDIA consumes government-provided outsourced ICT services, NDIA must obtain and assess relevant IRAP assessment reports for services that support DR, including any residual risks affecting recovery or data protection.
Third-party DR assurance, contracts and supplier conduct

Contract security terms and conditions are monitored and reviewed to ensure the specified security controls, terms and conditions are implemented, operated and maintained by the contracted provider, including any subcontractors, over the life of a contract.
Contract controls must be monitored throughout the contract lifecycle so DR capability does not degrade after onboarding or during operational change.
Applicable. NDIA must monitor ICT supplier compliance with DR/security controls across operations, changes, subcontracting and renewals.

NDIA must monitor, review and evidence that contracted ICT providers and subcontractors implement, operate and maintain agreed DR and security controls throughout the contract term, including periodic assurance, test results and remediation tracking.
Third-party DR assurance, contracts and supplier conduct
Security risks arising from contractual arrangements for the provision of goods and services are managed, reassessed and adjusted over the life of a contract.
Supplier risk changes as systems, threats and business needs change; DR policy needs lifecycle reassessment of external dependencies.
Applicable. NDIA must reassess outsourced, cloud and managed-service DR risks after major changes, incidents, tests or contract variations.

Security and DR risks arising from ICT contracts must be reassessed and adjusted over the life of the contract, including after significant changes, incidents, failed tests, threat changes or changes in supplier ownership/control.
Third-party DR assurance, contracts and supplier conduct
Secure and verifiable third-party vendors, providers, partners and associated services are used unless business operations require use, and the residual risks are managed and approved by the CISO.
DR policy must avoid unverifiable providers because untrusted dependencies can compromise recovery, data integrity and government information.
Applicable. NDIA must use secure and verifiable third parties for critical ICT, backup, cloud, data-centre and recovery services; exceptions require CISO approval.

NDIA must use secure and verifiable third-party vendors and associated services for ICT DR. Where business need requires an exception, residual security and recovery risks must be assessed, documented and approved by the CISO.
Critical services, BIA, RTO/RPO and service continuity scope
A business continuity plan is developed, implemented and maintained to respond effectively and minimise the impacts of significant business disruptions to the entity's critical services and assets.
Business continuity planning is the business authority for prioritising recovery of critical services and assets.
Applicable. NDIA requires ICT DR to support continuity of critical NDIS services, participant/provider channels, payments, data, contact-centre and corporate functions.
Business continuity alignment and critical services

NDIA must develop, maintain and test ICT DR arrangements that support the business continuity plan, prioritise critical services and assets, and minimise the impacts of significant disruptions in line with approved recovery objectives.
Critical services, BIA, RTO/RPO and service continuity scope
Plans for managing a broad range of emergencies are integrated within the business continuity plan.
Emergencies such as natural disasters, building loss, cyber attacks, supplier failures or pandemic events can require DR activation.
Applicable. NDIA ICT DR planning must cover broad emergency scenarios affecting people, facilities, technology, suppliers and communications.

The ICT DR Policy must define the emergency and disruption scenarios that can trigger DR, and must align ICT recovery procedures with emergency management, crisis management and business continuity arrangements.
Accessible, inclusive and properly marked DR communications and workarounds
Personnel who are likely to be impacted are notified if there is a heightened risk of an emergency.
Personnel notification prevents harm, enables remote or alternate operations and sets expectations during heightened risk.
Applicable. NDIA must notify ICT, security, supplier and business personnel who may be affected by, or required for, DR response.

NDIA must maintain notification processes for heightened emergency or disruption risk, including alerting affected personnel, recovery teams, business owners and suppliers of preparedness actions, access restrictions, alternate work arrangements and communications channels.
Backups, restoration, immutable recovery and transaction integrity
Entity implements operational controls for its information holdings that are proportional to their value, importance and sensitivity.
Recovery controls must match data value and sensitivity; backups and replicated environments may aggregate large volumes of personal and sensitive information.
Applicable. NDIA information holdings include sensitive participant, provider, financial and corporate data that require proportional operational controls in backup and recovery environments.
Information holdings, data criticality and backup protection

NDIA must classify and prioritise information holdings for DR and apply operational controls to production, backup, replicated, archived and recovered data proportionate to their value, importance, sensitivity and aggregation risk.
Baseline cyber controls for recovery readiness
The Australian Signals Directorate's Information Security Manual cyber security principles are applied during all stages of the lifecycle of each system.
DR must be designed into each system lifecycle stage; resilience, backups and recovery cannot be bolted on after implementation.
Applicable. NDIA ICT systems and platforms must apply ISM cyber security principles during design, build, operation, change, recovery and retirement.

NDIA must apply ASD ISM cyber security principles across the lifecycle of systems that support critical services, including requirements for secure architecture, backup, restoration, monitoring, change, decommissioning and DR test readiness.
Baseline cyber controls for recovery readiness
The Australian Signals Directorate's Information Security Manual controls and cyber security guidelines are applied on a risk-based approach.
DR controls should be selected from ISM guidance based on system risk, classification, business impact and threat profile.
Applicable. NDIA must apply ISM controls and guidelines on a risk basis for systems, networks, gateways, cloud services, backup platforms and recovery environments.

NDIA must apply ASD ISM controls and cyber security guidelines using a documented risk-based approach for all ICT DR capabilities, including protection of backups, privileged access, system hardening, logging, monitoring and secure recovery.
Architecture resilience, cloud/hosting assurance and physical dependencies

A Technology Asset Stocktake and Technology Security Risk Management Plan is created to identify and manage the entity's internet-facing systems or services to ensure continuous visibility and monitoring of the entity's resource and technology estate.
Continuous visibility of internet-facing systems is required to identify DR dependencies and manage vulnerable technologies that could cause or worsen outages.
Applicable. NDIA internet-facing portals, APIs, gateways and services must be represented in the technology asset stocktake and DR dependency register.
Technology asset stocktake and DR dependency register

NDIA must maintain a technology asset stocktake and technology security risk management plan for internet-facing systems and services, and use it to identify critical DR dependencies, recovery owners, monitoring coverage and risk treatments.
Architecture resilience, cloud/hosting assurance and physical dependencies

Outsourced facilities that house technology assets and their components with a catastrophic business impact level are certified by ASIO T4 physical security and accredited by ASD before they are used operationally.
Catastrophic-impact ICT assets require the highest assurance for outsourced physical facilities used for primary or DR hosting.

Conditional. Applies where NDIA technology assets or components in outsourced facilities have a catastrophic business impact level; otherwise use as a high-assurance criterion for critical DR facilities.
Outsourced facilities and high-impact DR hosting

Where NDIA uses outsourced facilities for technology assets with catastrophic business impact, the facilities must be ASIO-T4 certified and ASD-accredited before operational use. DR design must verify this before hosting or replication commences.
Governance, risk appetite, ownership and oversight

A cyber security strategy and uplift plan is developed, implemented and maintained to manage the entity's cyber security risks in accordance with the ISM and the Guiding Principles to Embed a Zero Trust Culture.
Cyber security strategy and uplift planning must drive DR resilience priorities, recovery capability improvement and remediation.
Applicable. NDIA ICT DR must align with its cyber strategy, uplift roadmap and Zero Trust-aligned controls for critical systems.
Cyber strategy alignment and resilience uplift

NDIA's ICT DR requirements, investment priorities and remediation actions must align with the cyber security strategy and uplift plan, the ISM and applicable Zero Trust principles, with progress tracked through governance reporting.
Backups, restoration, immutable recovery and transaction integrity
Regular back-ups mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Backups are a core DR control; Essential Eight Maturity Level Two defines a minimum cyber-resilience baseline for backup practices.
Applicable. NDIA must implement, protect and test backups for critical systems and data, including recovery from ransomware, corruption, deletion and supplier/platform failure.

NDIA must implement the Essential Eight Regular Backups mitigation strategy to at least Maturity Level Two for in-scope systems, including protected backup repositories, retention aligned to RPO/RTO, restoration testing and evidence of recoverability.
Baseline cyber controls for recovery readiness

The remaining mitigation strategies from the Strategies to Mitigate Cyber Security Incidents are considered and, where required, implemented to achieve an acceptable level of residual risk for their entity.
DR cannot rely on backups alone; additional cyber mitigations may be required to achieve acceptable residual risk.
Applicable. NDIA must consider other ASD mitigation strategies for resilience, such as patching, application control, MFA, hardening, monitoring and incident response.

NDIA must consider ASD's Strategies to Mitigate Cyber Security Incidents for ICT DR and implement additional mitigations where required to achieve acceptable residual risk for critical services and recovery environments.
Architecture resilience, cloud/hosting assurance and physical dependencies
Cloud Service Providers that have completed an IRAP assessment against the latest version of ASD's ISM within the previous 24 months are used.
Cloud services used for DR must have current independent assurance against the ISM; stale or absent IRAP reports create unacceptable recovery and data risk.
Applicable to cloud-hosted NDIA services and cloud-based backup/DR capabilities; only use CSPs with current IRAP evidence for relevant services.

NDIA must use cloud service providers for ICT DR only where the relevant cloud services have an IRAP assessment against the latest ISM within the previous 24 months and residual risks are accepted by the appropriate authority.
Third-party DR assurance, contracts and supplier conduct
Entities consider IRAP assessment recommendations and findings, and implement on a risk-based approach.
IRAP findings must influence risk treatments before services are relied on for recovery.
Applicable. NDIA must evaluate IRAP recommendations affecting confidentiality, integrity, availability, privileged access, logging, backups and recovery.
IRAP findings, risk treatment and acceptance

NDIA must review IRAP assessment reports for cloud and outsourced ICT services supporting DR, assess findings and recommendations, track remediation or compensating controls, and accept residual risks using NDIA risk governance.
Architecture resilience, cloud/hosting assurance and physical dependencies

Security classified or systems of government significance information and data is securely hosted using a Cloud Service Provider and Data Centre Provider that has been certified against the Australian Government Hosting Certification Framework.
Certified hosting ensures appropriate privacy, sovereignty and security controls for classified, Systems of Government Significance, sensitive or high-value data in primary and DR environments.

Conditional/applicable where NDIA systems store, process or recover security-classified, Systems of Government Significance, sensitive or high-value government data; use HCF-certified providers where required.
Certified cloud and data centre hosting

NDIA must host security-classified, declared Systems of Government Significance, sensitive and high-value government data used for ICT DR only with cloud and data centre providers certified under the Australian Government Hosting Certification Framework where required.
Architecture resilience, cloud/hosting assurance and physical dependencies
The Data Centre Facilities Supplies Panel is used when procuring certified data centre space and services.
DR procurement for data-centre space and services must use the approved government panel to maintain assurance and consistency.
Applicable for procuring data-centre space, colocation or related facilities used for NDIA primary hosting, replication or DR sites.
Data centre procurement and approved panels

When procuring certified data centre space or services for ICT production, backup, replication or DR environments, NDIA must use the Data Centre Facilities Supplies Panel or its successor mandatory whole-of-government procurement pathway.
Architecture resilience, cloud/hosting assurance and physical dependencies
Declared Systems of Government Significance are protected in accordance with the Australian Government Systems of Government Significance Standard.
Declared Systems of Government Significance require enhanced cyber obligations; DR policy must identify and protect any declared NDIA system accordingly.
Conditional. Applies if an NDIA system or service is declared a System of Government Significance; the DR policy should include a trigger to apply the SOGS Standard.

If an NDIA system is declared a System of Government Significance, NDIA must incorporate the Australian Government Systems of Government Significance Standard into DR requirements, resilience uplift, assurance, testing and reporting.
Architecture resilience, cloud/hosting assurance and physical dependencies

Physical security measures are implemented to minimise or remove the risk of information and physical asset resources being made inoperable or inaccessible, or being accessed, used or removed without appropriate authorisation.
DR fails if physical assets or information are inaccessible or inoperable; physical controls protect availability of ICT resources and recovery media.
Applicable. NDIA must protect ICT equipment, backup media, recovery work areas and facilities from unauthorised access, damage, loss or inoperability.
Physical protection of ICT and recovery resources

NDIA must implement physical security measures that minimise the risk of ICT information and physical assets becoming inoperable, inaccessible, unauthorisedly accessed, used, removed or damaged at production, backup and recovery locations.
Architecture resilience, cloud/hosting assurance and physical dependencies
Physical security measures are implemented to protect entity resources, commensurate with the assessed business impact level of their compromise, loss or damage.
Physical controls must scale with business impact; higher-impact systems need stronger controls at primary and alternate sites.
Applicable. NDIA must assess business impact for ICT assets and apply commensurate physical protections for production, backup, DR and recovery operations.
Business impact level and physical security controls

Physical security for NDIA ICT assets, backup media, network equipment, data-centre services and recovery facilities must be commensurate with the assessed business impact level of compromise, loss, damage or unavailability.
Governance, risk appetite, ownership and oversight
Directs Australian Government entities to adhere to the Commonwealth Technology Standard.
DR policy must align technology governance, lifecycle and operational resilience with mandatory technology management expectations.
Applicable to NDIA where the Direction/Standard is in scope or adopted as Commonwealth baseline.

- ICT DR architectures must align with applicable Commonwealth technology management requirements.
- New or changed systems must consider DR, recoverability and exit arrangements before production approval.
Protective Security Directions, PSPF Standards and Commonwealth Technology Standard
Protective security direction, standard and technology standard
Governance, risk appetite, ownership and oversight
Sets requirements for technology management across government systems.
DR capability should be embedded into system design, lifecycle management, operational support and change control.
Applicable to NDIA ICT systems and platforms, especially high-value government data and critical digital services.

- All material technology changes must assess impacts on DR design, backup, monitoring, recovery procedures and RTO/RPO achievement.
- Systems must not go live without approved and tested recovery arrangements proportionate to criticality.
Protective Security Directions, PSPF Standards and Commonwealth Technology Standard
Protective security direction, standard and technology standard
Critical services, BIA, RTO/RPO and service continuity scope
Applies extra expectations to systems assessed as significant to government operations.
DR policy must identify high-consequence systems and apply heightened assurance, recovery and reporting requirements.
Conditionally applicable if NDIA systems are designated or assessed as systems of government significance.

- NDIA must identify systems requiring elevated recovery assurance because of participant, financial, privacy, whole-of-government or public trust impacts.
- Critical systems must have enhanced recovery testing, executive reporting and supplier assurance.
Protective Security Directions, PSPF Standards and Commonwealth Technology Standard
Protective security direction, standard and technology standard
Architecture resilience, cloud/hosting assurance and physical dependencies
Sets expectations for gateway services protecting government networks and systems.
DR depends on secure connectivity; alternate networks and recovery access must maintain gateway protections.
Applicable to NDIA internet gateways, secure remote access, inter-agency connections and cloud connectivity used in recovery.

- Alternate connectivity used during recovery must maintain approved gateway, monitoring and access controls.
- Emergency network changes must be documented, approved, time-limited and reverted or normalised after recovery.
Protective Security Directions, PSPF Standards and Commonwealth Technology Standard
Protective security direction, standard and technology standard
Accessible, inclusive and properly marked DR communications and workarounds
Australian Government Email Protective Marking Standard 2025
Standardises protective markings for Australian Government email.
Incident and recovery communications may contain sensitive information and need correct markings and distribution controls.
Applicable to NDIA email and collaboration communications during DR events.

- DR communications containing sensitive or classified information must use appropriate protective markings.
- Distribution lists and external communications during incidents must be checked before sensitive information is sent.
Protective Security Directions, PSPF Standards and Commonwealth Technology Standard
Protective security direction, standard and technology standard
Critical services, BIA, RTO/RPO and service continuity scope
Business continuity and disaster recovery plans support continued operations and recovery after incidents.
This is the direct Australian Government cyber principle for ICT DR and business continuity integration.
Highly applicable to NDIA critical ICT services and participant information systems.

- NDIA must maintain ICT DR plans that support continued operation or timely recovery of critical services after cyber, technology, supplier or facilities incidents.
- DR plans must be aligned with business continuity, cyber incident response and crisis management arrangements.
Australian Signals Directorate / Australian Cyber Security Centre
Backups, restoration, immutable recovery and transaction integrity
ISM - data backup and restoration guidance
Requires appropriate backup, restoration and protection practices for important data and systems.
Backups are the foundation of recovery from ransomware, data corruption, accidental deletion and system failure.
Applicable to all NDIA production data, configuration, identity, security logs and critical supporting services.

- Critical NDIA systems must have documented backup schedules, retention, protection, restoration procedures and recovery verification.
- Backup restoration must be tested regularly and failures remediated as operational risks.
Australian Signals Directorate / Australian Cyber Security Centre
Critical services, BIA, RTO/RPO and service continuity scope
ISM - service continuity for online services
Requires continuity controls for important online services and supporting infrastructure.
NDIA public-facing and staff-facing services need resilient architecture and monitored service continuity.
Applicable to participant, provider, staff, integration and public information services.

- Systems within ICT DR scope must be designed for resilience commensurate with their criticality and agreed service levels.
- Single points of failure affecting critical NDIA services must be identified, risk-assessed and treated.
Australian Signals Directorate / Australian Cyber Security Centre
DR activation, cyber recovery, ransomware response and breach notification
ISM - cyber security incident response integration
Requires planning and procedures for detecting, reporting, responding to and recovering from cyber security incidents.
Cyber incidents often trigger DR; the policy must join incident containment with safe recovery and evidence preservation.
Applicable to cyber events affecting NDIA systems, cloud services, identity, endpoints, backups and suppliers.

- Cyber recovery must not restore compromised systems into service until containment, eradication and assurance steps have been completed.
- Recovery decisions must preserve forensic evidence and security logs where required.
Australian Signals Directorate / Australian Cyber Security Centre
DR testing, audit, accessibility validation and remediation tracking
ISM March 2026 - system recovery assurance principle
Emphasises assurance that systems can be recovered securely and effectively after compromise or disruption.
DR policy needs explicit assurance, test evidence and lessons-learned cycles, not just documented plans.
Applicable to all NDIA critical systems and high-value data services.

- NDIA must periodically verify that critical systems can be recovered to a trusted state within agreed recovery objectives.
- Recovery tests must include technical validation, business validation, security validation and remediation tracking.
Australian Signals Directorate / Australian Cyber Security Centre
Backups, restoration, immutable recovery and transaction integrity
